paragraphs.heading: What it says
paragraphs.text: The Chinese remainder theorem is about remainders. Suppose you divide an unknown whole number n by several divisors and learn only the remainder each time. If no two of the divisors have a shared factor other than 1, a condition called pairwise coprime, those remainders pin down exactly one remainder for n when it is divided by the product of all the divisors.

paragraphs.heading: A worked example
paragraphs.text: Take a number that leaves 2 when divided by 3, 3 when divided by 5, and 2 when divided by 7. Nothing else about it is known. Even so, its remainder on division by 105, which is 3 × 5 × 7, is settled: it is 23. And 23 is the one positive value below 105 that fits all three conditions.

paragraphs.heading: An old puzzle
paragraphs.text: The same example appears as a puzzle in the work of Sunzi: some things of unknown number leave two over when counted in threes, three over when counted in fives, and two over when counted in sevens. Sunzi posed only this one problem, with no method and no proof, so by modern standards it is not a theorem. Aryabhata described a way to solve this problem in the 6th century, and special cases were known to Brahmagupta in the 7th century and appear in Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202. Qin Jiushao gave a complete solution, called Da-yan-shu, in a treatise of 1247.

paragraphs.heading: The general statement
paragraphs.text: In general terms, pick divisors n₁, ..., nₖ, each greater than 1, often called moduli, and let N be their product. Suppose the moduli are pairwise coprime and you choose target remainders a₁, ..., aₖ with 0 ≤ aᵢ < nᵢ. Then there is exactly one whole number x with 0 ≤ x < N that leaves remainder aᵢ on division by nᵢ, for every i.

paragraphs.heading: Why the answer is unique
paragraphs.text: The uniqueness part has a short argument. If x and y both satisfy every condition, they leave the same remainders, so x − y is a multiple of each modulus. Because the moduli are pairwise coprime, their product N divides x − y as well. If x and y are both non-negative and smaller than N, that forces x = y.

paragraphs.heading: Splitting big sums
paragraphs.text: The theorem is a workhorse for computing with large integers. Instead of one calculation whose result is known to stay below some bound, you can do several matching calculations with small integers, one for each modulus, and then rebuild the answer. This can be much faster than working directly when N and the number of operations are large. Under the name multi-modular computation, it is used widely in linear algebra done with integers or rational numbers.
